subject: histology
prompt: A light-microscopy stain shows a basement membrane beneath an epithelium. Which statement best distinguishes it from the basal lamina?

options.text: The basement membrane includes the epithelial basal lamina plus an underlying reticular lamina
The basement membrane is only the lamina lucida, whereas the basal lamina is only the lamina densa
The basal lamina is made by fibroblasts, whereas the basement membrane is made only by epithelial cells
The terms describe two unrelated structures on opposite surfaces of an epithelial cell

explanation: The basal lamina is an epithelial extracellular-matrix layer; the light-microscopic basement membrane includes it together with the connective-tissue reticular lamina.

distractorExplanations.B: Lamina lucida and lamina densa are subdivisions associated with the basal lamina, not the stated distinction.
distractorExplanations.C: The production relationship is reversed and oversimplified: epithelial cells contribute basal-lamina components, while connective-tissue cells contribute the reticular lamina.
distractorExplanations.D: Both structures are at the basal interface and are closely related.

learningObjective: Differentiate basal lamina from the light-microscopic basement membrane.

source.title: EPITHELIAL TISSUE.pdf
source.excerpt: Basal lamina versus basement membrane lecture distinction.

subject: histology
prompt: Which molecular linkage most directly connects the zonula adherens of one epithelial cell to the actin cytoskeleton of its neighbor?

options.text: Cadherins linked intracellularly through catenins to actin filaments
Connexins assembled into connexons and linked to microtubules
Integrins linked through plakins to intermediate filaments
Claudins and occludins linked directly to keratin filaments

explanation: In a zonula adherens, transmembrane cadherins bind across the intercellular space and catenins connect them to cortical actin.

distractorExplanations.B: Connexins form gap junction channels, not adherens junctions.
distractorExplanations.C: Integrin–intermediate filament linkage describes a hemidesmosome at the basal surface.
distractorExplanations.D: Claudins and occludins are characteristic of tight junctions; they do not form the adherens belt.

learningObjective: Identify the cadherin–catenin–actin architecture of the zonula adherens.

subject: histology
prompt: A gap-junction channel spanning two adjacent epithelial cells is formed by the alignment of two connexons. What is each connexon?

options.text: A hexamer of connexin proteins
A tetramer of claudin proteins
A pair of cadherin dimers
A ring of six integrin heterodimers

explanation: Each hemichannel, or connexon, is assembled from six connexin subunits; connexons in adjacent cells align to form the communicating channel.

distractorExplanations.B: Claudins form sealing strands in tight junctions.
distractorExplanations.C: Cadherins mediate adhesion but do not form the aqueous gap-junction pore.
distractorExplanations.D: Integrins mediate cell–matrix adhesion rather than forming intercellular channels.

learningObjective: Recall the subunit organization of a gap-junction connexon.

subject: histology
prompt: Where are myoepithelial cells located in an exocrine gland, and what is their principal role?

options.text: Between secretory or duct cells and the basal lamina; they contract to help expel secretion
Within the gland lumen; they propel secretion by motile cilia
In the surrounding connective tissue; they synthesize the reticular lamina
At the apical surface of acinar cells; they seal the lumen with tight junctions

explanation: Myoepithelial cells lie inside the basal lamina but outside the secretory/duct epithelial cells. Their contractile processes help squeeze secretory products into ducts.

distractorExplanations.B: They are basal, contractile cells rather than luminal ciliated cells.
distractorExplanations.C: They are epithelial in position and contractile in function, not connective-tissue matrix cells.
distractorExplanations.D: They do not occupy the apical junctional complex.

learningObjective: State the position and function of glandular myoepithelial cells.

subject: histology
prompt: Which combination best identifies a plasma cell in connective tissue?

options.text: Eccentric clock-face nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm, and a pale perinuclear Golgi zone
Central multilobed nucleus with fine neutral granules
Kidney-shaped nucleus with abundant lysosomes and pseudopodia
Round central nucleus surrounded by a single large lipid droplet

explanation: An antibody-secreting plasma cell has abundant rough ER, producing basophilia; its eccentric nucleus shows cartwheel chromatin and its prominent Golgi appears as a pale hof.

distractorExplanations.B: This describes a neutrophil.
distractorExplanations.C: This is closer to a macrophage/monocyte phenotype.
distractorExplanations.D: This describes a unilocular adipocyte, not a plasma cell.

learningObjective: Recognize the classic light-microscopic features of a plasma cell.

subject: histology
prompt: In an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, which event most directly triggers mast-cell degranulation?

options.text: Cross-linking of FcεRI-bound IgE by a multivalent antigen
Binding of IgG to collagen type I fibrils
Phagocytosis of an erythrocyte through Fcγ receptors
Recognition of antigen by a plasma-cell surface immunoglobulin

explanation: Antigen cross-links IgE already bound to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on the mast-cell surface, initiating release of histamine and other mediators.

distractorExplanations.B: IgG–collagen binding is not the canonical trigger for immediate mast-cell degranulation.
distractorExplanations.C: Mast cells are not principally activated by erythrophagocytosis.
distractorExplanations.D: Plasma cells secrete antibody; this does not describe the mast-cell trigger.

learningObjective: Explain the IgE-dependent trigger for mast-cell degranulation.

subject: histology
prompt: Which sequence correctly follows collagen synthesis from the fibroblast to formation of an extracellular fibril?

options.text: Hydroxylation and glycosylation → procollagen triple helix → secretion → cleavage of terminal propeptides → fibril assembly
Terminal-propeptide cleavage in rough ER → secretion of tropocollagen → hydroxylation outside the cell → fibril assembly
Triple-helix formation in the Golgi → extracellular glycosylation → secretion → intracellular cross-linking
Fibril assembly in secretory vesicles → exocytosis → conversion of collagen to procollagen outside the cell

explanation: Pro-α chains are hydroxylated and glycosylated in the cell, assemble as procollagen, and are secreted. Extracellular procollagen peptidases remove terminal propeptides, allowing tropocollagen fibril assembly and cross-linking.

distractorExplanations.B: Propeptide cleavage is extracellular, whereas hydroxylation occurs intracellularly before secretion.
distractorExplanations.C: Triple-helix formation begins in the rough ER, and glycosylation is not solely extracellular.
distractorExplanations.D: Fibrils do not normally assemble within secretory vesicles; procollagen is the secreted soluble precursor.

learningObjective: Order the intracellular and extracellular stages of collagen fibril formation.

subject: histology
prompt: Which description correctly relates a glycosaminoglycan (GAG), a proteoglycan monomer, and a proteoglycan aggregate?

options.text: GAG chains attach to a core protein to form a proteoglycan monomer; many monomers can bind a hyaluronan backbone
A core protein attaches to collagen to form a GAG; many GAGs then make hyaluronan
Hyaluronan is covalently attached to every core protein and is itself a sulfated GAG
Proteoglycan aggregates are formed only from fibronectin and laminin without carbohydrate chains

explanation: Most proteoglycan monomers consist of sulfated GAG chains on a core protein. Large aggregates form when many monomers associate noncovalently with a hyaluronan backbone via link proteins.

distractorExplanations.B: The hierarchy is reversed: GAG chains are carbohydrate components of proteoglycans.
distractorExplanations.C: Hyaluronan is nonsulfated and generally serves as the long backbone through noncovalent interactions.
distractorExplanations.D: Fibronectin and laminin are adhesive glycoproteins, not the sole components of proteoglycan aggregates.

learningObjective: Distinguish GAGs, proteoglycan monomers, and proteoglycan aggregates.

subject: histology
prompt: Nissl substance is abundant in the neuronal soma and proximal dendrites but is absent from which site?

options.text: Axon hillock and axon
Perikaryal cytoplasm around the nucleus
Proximal dendritic cytoplasm
Regions containing rough endoplasmic reticulum

explanation: Nissl substance represents rough ER and free polyribosomes. It is present in the soma and dendrites but absent from the axon hillock and axon.

distractorExplanations.B: The soma contains abundant Nissl substance.
distractorExplanations.C: Proximal dendrites can contain Nissl substance.
distractorExplanations.D: Rough ER is the structural basis of Nissl substance.

learningObjective: Use Nissl distribution to distinguish the axon hillock from soma and dendrites.

subject: histology
prompt: Which pairing of axonal transport direction and motor protein is correct?

options.text: Kinesin: anterograde toward the terminal; dynein: retrograde toward the soma
Dynein: anterograde toward the terminal; kinesin: retrograde toward the soma
Kinesin: both directions along actin; myosin: retrograde along microtubules
Myosin: anterograde along microtubules; dynein: both directions along actin

explanation: Microtubule-based kinesin generally carries cargo anterogradely toward the axon terminal, whereas cytoplasmic dynein mediates retrograde transport toward the cell body.

distractorExplanations.B: The motors are reversed.
distractorExplanations.C: Fast axonal transport is chiefly microtubule-based, not a kinesin-on-actin system.
distractorExplanations.D: Myosin is an actin motor and does not replace kinesin as the main anterograde microtubule motor.

learningObjective: Match kinesin and dynein with the direction of axonal transport.

subject: histology
prompt: Which structural feature provides the principal diffusion barrier of the blood–brain barrier?

options.text: Continuous capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions
Fenestrated capillary endothelial cells covered only by astrocyte processes
A continuous layer of ependymal cells around every CNS capillary
Pericytes joined by gap junctions that completely replace endothelial junctions

explanation: The core barrier is the nonfenestrated continuous endothelium sealed by tight junctions. Its basal lamina, pericytes, and astrocytic end-feet support and regulate the barrier but do not replace the endothelial seal.

distractorExplanations.B: CNS capillaries are characteristically nonfenestrated, and astrocyte end-feet are supportive rather than the primary seal.
distractorExplanations.C: Ependymal cells line ventricles and the central canal, not every capillary.
distractorExplanations.D: Pericytes contribute to barrier regulation, but endothelial tight junctions are the principal diffusion barrier.

learningObjective: Identify the cellular structure chiefly responsible for the blood–brain barrier.

subject: histology
prompt: Which mapping of connective-tissue sheath to peripheral-nerve structure is correct?

options.text: Endoneurium surrounds individual nerve fibers; perineurium surrounds fascicles; epineurium surrounds the whole nerve
Endoneurium surrounds fascicles; perineurium surrounds the whole nerve; epineurium surrounds individual axons
Perineurium surrounds individual fibers; endoneurium surrounds fascicles; epineurium surrounds nodes of Ranvier
Epineurium surrounds individual Schwann cells; perineurium surrounds myelin lamellae; endoneurium surrounds the whole nerve

explanation: Endoneurium is the delicate connective tissue around individual fibers, perineurium forms the cellular sheath of each fascicle, and epineurium encloses and binds the entire nerve.

distractorExplanations.B: This reverses all three levels.
distractorExplanations.C: The perineurium belongs around fascicles, not individual fibers.
distractorExplanations.D: Myelin is produced by Schwann cells; these connective-tissue sheaths are not arranged as stated.

learningObjective: Map endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium to their anatomical levels.

subject: histology
prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts interstitial and appositional growth of cartilage?

options.text: Interstitial growth results from division of chondrocytes within the matrix; appositional growth results from chondrogenic cells in the perichondrium adding tissue at the surface
Interstitial growth occurs only from perichondrial osteoblasts; appositional growth occurs from isogenous groups deep in cartilage
Both mechanisms require blood vessels to enter lacunae and directly supply dividing chondrocytes
Appositional growth is the only mechanism in articular cartilage because it has a thick perichondrium

explanation: Interstitial growth expands cartilage from within through chondrocyte division and matrix secretion. Appositional growth adds cartilage at the surface from chondrogenic cells of the perichondrium.

distractorExplanations.B: The cellular sources are reversed.
distractorExplanations.C: Cartilage is avascular; chondrocytes receive nutrients by diffusion.
distractorExplanations.D: Articular cartilage lacks a perichondrium, so it cannot grow appositionally from that source.

learningObjective: Differentiate interstitial from appositional cartilage growth.

subject: histology
prompt: Which combination is most characteristic of fibrocartilage?

options.text: Thick bundles of type I collagen, chondrocytes in rows, and no perichondrium
A glassy matrix rich in type II collagen, isogenous groups, and a perichondrium at every surface
A dense network of elastic fibers and a mineralized perichondrium
Type IV collagen sheets surrounding adipocytes and abundant fenestrated capillaries

explanation: Fibrocartilage combines features of dense connective tissue and cartilage: prominent type I collagen bundles, chondrocytes often aligned in rows, and absence of perichondrium.

distractorExplanations.B: This is closer to hyaline cartilage, and articular hyaline cartilage still lacks perichondrium.
distractorExplanations.C: Elastic cartilage has elastic fibers but is not characterized by a mineralized perichondrium.
distractorExplanations.D: Type IV collagen forms basal laminae, not the principal matrix of fibrocartilage.

learningObjective: Recognize the matrix and covering features of fibrocartilage.

subject: histology
prompt: Which feature best distinguishes Volkmann canals from Haversian canals in compact bone?

options.text: Volkmann canals run transversely or obliquely, connect osteonal canals, and are not surrounded by concentric lamellae
Volkmann canals lie at the center of every osteon and are surrounded by concentric lamellae
Volkmann canals contain only osteocytes, whereas Haversian canals contain only marrow
Volkmann canals are microscopic channels between lacunae through which osteocyte processes pass

explanation: Haversian canals run longitudinally at osteon centers and are surrounded by concentric lamellae. Volkmann canals cross between them and are not themselves centers of osteons.

distractorExplanations.B: This describes a Haversian canal.
distractorExplanations.C: Both canal types carry vessels and nerves; neither is defined by containing only osteocytes or marrow.
distractorExplanations.D: Canaliculi, not Volkmann canals, connect lacunae and contain osteocyte processes.

learningObjective: Distinguish perforating Volkmann canals from central Haversian canals.

source.title: BONE&JOINT TISSUE.pdf
source.excerpt: Haversian versus Volkmann canals lecture distinction.

subject: histology
prompt: Which pairing correctly describes the two principal synovial-lining cell types?

options.text: Type A cells are macrophage-like and phagocytic; type B cells are fibroblast-like and synthesize hyaluronan and other matrix components
Type A cells secrete immunoglobulin; type B cells resorb bone with a ruffled border
Type A cells produce myelin; type B cells form the articular cartilage perichondrium
Type A cells are endothelial; type B cells are smooth-muscle cells that pump synovial fluid

explanation: Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-derived phagocytic cells. Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like secretory cells that contribute hyaluronan and lubricating components to synovial fluid.

distractorExplanations.B: These functions describe plasma cells and osteoclasts, not synoviocytes.
distractorExplanations.C: Synoviocytes neither myelinate nerves nor create a perichondrium over articular cartilage.
distractorExplanations.D: The synovial intima is not an endothelial–smooth muscle pump.

learningObjective: Differentiate type A and type B synoviocytes by origin and function.

subject: histology
prompt: Keratinocyte lamellar granules contribute most directly to which epidermal function?

options.text: Formation of the extracellular lipid water barrier in the stratum granulosum
Synthesis of melanin in the stratum basale
Antigen presentation by Langerhans cells
Anchoring the epidermis to the reticular dermis with type I collagen

explanation: Lamellar granules release lipid-rich contents between cells of the upper granular layer, helping create the permeability barrier that limits transepidermal water loss.

distractorExplanations.B: Melanin is synthesized in melanocytes, not in keratinocyte lamellar granules.
distractorExplanations.C: Langerhans cells perform antigen presentation.
distractorExplanations.D: Type I collagen is a major dermal matrix component; the epidermal attachment involves the basement-membrane zone.

learningObjective: Explain the role of lamellar granules in the epidermal water barrier.

subject: histology
prompt: Which epidermal cell pairing of origin and usual location is correct?

options.text: Melanocyte: neural crest, mainly stratum basale; Langerhans cell: bone marrow, mainly stratum spinosum
Melanocyte: bone marrow, mainly stratum corneum; Langerhans cell: neural crest, mainly stratum basale
Merkel cell: mesoderm, mainly stratum granulosum; keratinocyte: neural crest, mainly dermis
Langerhans cell: epidermal ectoderm, mainly stratum lucidum; melanocyte: endoderm, mainly dermis

explanation: Melanocytes derive from neural crest and occupy the basal layer. Langerhans cells are bone-marrow-derived antigen-presenting cells found mainly among spinous-layer keratinocytes.

distractorExplanations.B: The origins and typical layers are reversed or incorrect.
distractorExplanations.C: Keratinocytes arise from surface ectoderm and remain epidermal; Merkel cells are basal mechanosensory cells.
distractorExplanations.D: Neither stated embryologic origin is correct, and melanocytes normally reside in the epidermal basal layer.

learningObjective: Match melanocytes and Langerhans cells with their origin and epidermal location.

subject: histology
prompt: A skin specimen has a very thick stratum corneum and a distinct stratum lucidum. Which additional finding should be expected?

options.text: Numerous eccrine sweat glands but no hair follicles or sebaceous glands
Numerous hair follicles and sebaceous glands but no sweat glands
A thin epidermis with no dermal papillae
Apocrine glands opening directly onto the surface throughout the specimen

explanation: Thick skin of palms and soles has a thick epidermis with stratum lucidum and abundant eccrine sweat glands, but it lacks hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

distractorExplanations.B: Hair follicles and sebaceous glands characterize thin, hairy skin.
distractorExplanations.C: Thick skin has prominent epidermal ridges and dermal papillae.
distractorExplanations.D: Apocrine glands are regional and usually open into hair follicles; they are not the defining gland of thick skin.

learningObjective: Use appendage distribution to distinguish thick from thin skin.

source.title: SKIN.pptx
source.excerpt: Thick versus thin skin lecture distinction.

subject: histology
prompt: Which statement correctly describes the major vascular plexuses of the skin?

options.text: A deep plexus lies near the dermis–hypodermis junction, and a superficial plexus lies in the papillary region and supplies capillary loops
The epidermis contains a dense superficial plexus, while the dermis is avascular
Both plexuses are confined to the stratum basale and directly contact keratinocytes
A superficial arterial plexus lies in the stratum corneum, and a deep venous plexus lies inside hair shafts

explanation: The avascular epidermis is nourished by diffusion from dermal vessels. A deep cutaneous plexus is near the dermis–hypodermis boundary, and a superficial/subpapillary plexus sends capillary loops into dermal papillae.

distractorExplanations.B: The epidermis is avascular; dermis contains the vascular networks.
distractorExplanations.C: Vessels do not enter the epidermis.
distractorExplanations.D: Neither the stratum corneum nor hair shafts contains vascular plexuses.

learningObjective: Locate the superficial and deep vascular plexuses of skin.

subject: histology
prompt: In systemic capillaries, erythrocyte Band 3 protein supports carbon dioxide transport by exchanging which ions?

options.text: Intracellular bicarbonate for extracellular chloride
Intracellular sodium for extracellular potassium
Intracellular calcium for extracellular magnesium
Intracellular hydrogen for extracellular sodium

explanation: Band 3 (AE1) exchanges bicarbonate out of the erythrocyte for chloride into it in systemic tissues, maintaining electroneutrality during the chloride shift.

distractorExplanations.B: The sodium–potassium gradient is maintained mainly by Na+/K+-ATPase, not Band 3.
distractorExplanations.C: Band 3 is not a calcium–magnesium exchanger.
distractorExplanations.D: Hydrogen handling is linked to hemoglobin buffering; Band 3 specifically mediates chloride–bicarbonate exchange.

learningObjective: Relate erythrocyte Band 3 to the chloride shift.

subject: histology
prompt: Which set correctly matches normal human hemoglobins with their globin-chain composition?

options.text: HbA: α2β2; HbA2: α2δ2; HbF: α2γ2
HbA: α2γ2; HbA2: α2β2; HbF: α2δ2
HbA: β4; HbA2: γ4; HbF: α4
HbA: αβ; HbA2: αδ; HbF: αγ

explanation: The major adult hemoglobin HbA is α2β2, minor adult HbA2 is α2δ2, and fetal hemoglobin HbF is α2γ2.

distractorExplanations.B: This incorrectly swaps the beta, delta, and gamma pairings.
distractorExplanations.C: Normal hemoglobins are tetramers with two pairs of globin chains, not the listed homotetramers.
distractorExplanations.D: The formulas omit the tetrameric two-plus-two composition.

learningObjective: Recall the globin-chain composition of HbA, HbA2, and HbF.

subject: histology
prompt: Which platelet structure–content pairing is correct?

options.text: Peripheral hyalomere: microtubule marginal bundle; alpha granules: fibrinogen and platelet-derived growth factor; dense granules: ADP and calcium
Central granulomere: hemoglobin; alpha granules: histamine only; dense granules: collagen type I
Peripheral hyalomere: nucleus and rough ER; alpha granules: DNA; dense granules: myelin basic protein
Open canalicular system: actin-free lipid droplets; alpha granules: bile salts; dense granules: thyroxine

explanation: The pale peripheral hyalomere contains the cytoskeleton including the marginal microtubule bundle. The central granulomere contains alpha granules with adhesive/growth proteins and dense granules rich in ADP, ATP, calcium, and serotonin.

distractorExplanations.B: Platelets lack hemoglobin-rich granulomeres, and the granule contents are wrong.
distractorExplanations.C: Platelets are anucleate and do not store DNA or myelin protein in their granules.
distractorExplanations.D: The open canalicular system communicates with the surface and supports secretion; the listed contents are unrelated.

learningObjective: Distinguish platelet structural zones and major granule contents.

source.title: Blood& HEM.pdf
source.excerpt: Platelet zones and granules lecture distinction.

subject: histology
prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes neutrophil primary from secondary granules?

options.text: Primary azurophilic granules contain myeloperoxidase and lysosomal enzymes; secondary specific granules contain lactoferrin and lysozyme
Primary granules contain hemoglobin; secondary granules contain immunoglobulin
Primary granules contain histamine and heparin; secondary granules contain major basic protein
Primary granules contain insulin; secondary granules contain collagen type II

explanation: Primary azurophilic granules are lysosome-like and contain myeloperoxidase, acid hydrolases, and antimicrobial proteins. Secondary specific granules include lactoferrin, lysozyme, and other antimicrobial components.

distractorExplanations.B: Hemoglobin is an erythrocyte protein, and neutrophils do not store immunoglobulin as their defining granule contents.
distractorExplanations.C: Histamine/heparin suggest basophil or mast-cell granules; major basic protein is characteristic of eosinophils.
distractorExplanations.D: These substances are unrelated to neutrophil granules.

learningObjective: Differentiate the characteristic contents of primary and secondary neutrophil granules.
